reason: The provided sources support 14 claims backed by at least two independent domains regarding Cassiopeia A's distance, explosion type, discovery, and physical structure.
story: About 11,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia lies Cassiopeia A, the youngest known supernova remnant in the Milky Way. When its massive progenitor star exhausted its nuclear fuel in the late 17th century, its core collapsed and violently hurled its outer layers into space at thousands of kilometers per second. Despite creating an explosion of immense energy, its optical light was heavily dimmed by thick interstellar dust lanes, leaving almost no historical record on Earth—except possibly a single cataloging note by astronomer John Flamsteed in 1680. Centered on a rapidly cooling neutron star discovered by the Chandra X-Ray Observatory, the expanding remnant forms an asymmetric shell rich in silicon, sulfur, and other heavy elements. Centuries after the direct blast passed Earth, astronomers analyzed light echoes reflected off surrounding dust, confirming that the catastrophe was an asymmetric Type IIb supernova from a shredded red supergiant.
angle: Light from one of the youngest supernova explosions in our galaxy reached Earth in the 1600s, but thick interstellar dust cloaked the blast, leaving almost no historical record.

claims.claim: Cassiopeia A is the youngest known supernova remnant in the Milky Way galaxy.
Cassiopeia A is located approximately 11,000 light-years (3.4 kiloparsecs) away from Earth.
Cassiopeia A is situated in the constellation Cassiopeia.
Light from the Cassiopeia A supernova explosion first reached Earth in the late 17th century, around 1680.
Astronomer John Flamsteed may have recorded the supernova on August 16, 1680, as a sixth-magnitude star named 3 Cassiopeiae.
Interstellar dust along the line of sight absorbed optical light, hiding the supernova from clear naked-eye observation.
The Cassiopeia A progenitor explosion was a Type IIb supernova.
The progenitor star was a red supergiant that had lost most of its outer hydrogen envelope prior to core collapse.
Astronomers identified the supernova classification by analyzing light echoes reflected off nearby interstellar dust clouds.
The Chandra X-Ray Observatory discovered a central compact object (a neutron star) at the geometric center of Cassiopeia A in 1999.
The stellar debris ejected during the explosion contains heavy chemical elements including sulfur and silicon.
The outer expanding shell of Cassiopeia A moves outward at speeds of thousands of kilometers per second.
The supernova explosion ejected stellar material asymmetrically rather than in a uniform sphere.
The expanding remnant shell measures approximately 10 to 13 light-years across.

disputed: Whether John Flamsteed's 1680 catalog entry for 3 Cassiopeiae was a direct observation of the supernova, a position measurement error, or a transient star is uncertain; the script should frame this as a potential candidate observation.
The claim that the 1630 noon day star associated with Charles II was Cassiopeia A is widely doubted in favor of Venus; the script should leave this detail out.
Source estimates for the expansion shell diameter differ slightly (10 light-years in S1 vs 13 light-years / 4 parsecs in S2); the script should state roughly 10 to 13 light-years.
